definitions.definition: The Goddess herself as the power of the absolute; without her even Śiva cannot stir (SL 1; Subhagodaya). For Śāktas she is the supreme reality, the Mother, identical with Brahman.
Consciousness-power (citśakti) and also the power of the insentient (LSN 90); the self-awareness (vimarśa) in which Śiva's light knows itself (Kāmakalāvilāsa 2); Lalitā in union with Kāmeśvara.

equivalents.note: Śāktas call māyā the Goddess's own power; Advaita treats māyā as indeterminable and ultimately unreal

definitions.definition: The Goddess; for Śāktas the supreme deity, called Mahādevī, Parā Śakti, Ambikā, of whom all goddesses are forms (Devī Māhātmya 11).
The Mother: the Goddess addressed as mother of all; Lalitā as Śrīmātā (LSN 1) and Lalitāmbikā (LSN 183).
The supreme Goddess of Śrīvidyā, 'she who plays': Mahātripurasundarī, seated on Kāmeśvara's lap in the Śrīcakra, whose form is the oneness of Śiva and Śakti (LSN 183).

equivalents.note: Lalitā is Brahman, nirguṇa and saguṇa

definitions.definition: 'The beauty of the three cities': the Goddess of Śrīvidyā; as Mahātripurasundarī the queen of Mahākāmeśa (LSN 57).

literal: beautiful one of the three cities

definitions.definition: The Goddess as she who is prior (purā) to every triad — abodes, principles, seats, liṅgas, letters — the fusion of light and self-awareness (Amṛtānanda on YH 1.6); she 'whose city is threefold' (triangle, circle and square; the three-part mantra) in Bhāskararāya's gloss.
She who existed before the three lights (Naṭanānanda's Cidvallī on Kāmakalāvilāsa 2).

literal: she of the three cities / prior to the three

definitions.definition: 'Sovereign of the king of kings': Lalitā as supreme empress, the form worshipped in South Indian Śrīvidyā temples.

literal: queen of the king of kings

definitions.definition: 'Lord of desire': Śiva as Lalitā's consort, seated in the bindu of the Śrīcakra with the Goddess on his lap (LSN 21; PKS 4.5).
The Goddess as Kāmeśvara's consort; also the first of the fifteen Nityās and one of the three goddesses of the inner triangle (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad: the unmanifest).
The supreme Goddess; in the Kalpasūtra one of the vidyās worshipped (the eighth section, parākrama); the commentators call Mahātripurasundarī Parābhaṭṭārikā.
Both the fifteen-syllable mantra of Lalitā (with its sixteen-syllable form) and the tradition of her worship; the Goddess is herself 'Śrīvidyā, the sixteen-syllable vidyā, three-peaked' (LSN 118).
Auspicious good fortune and conjugal felicity, the worldly and spiritual blessing the Goddess grants; hence 'Saubhāgya-vidyā' and titles such as Saubhāgyabhāskara.

The 'king of cakras', Lalitā's dwelling (LSN 182): nine interlocking triangles — four of Śiva, five of Śakti — with the central point, forty-three angles, the eight- and sixteen-petalled lotuses, three circles and the square of three lines (SL 11); it arises when the supreme Śakti beholds her own vibrancy (YH 1.9-10); the body itself is the Śrīcakra (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
For the Samayins the Śrīcakra is worshipped only in the inner space and is the moon-disc in the crown lotus (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 10).
The Śrīcakra built in raised, three-dimensional form (meru-prastāra), as distinct from the flat form (bhū-prastāra).

An 'enclosure' of the Śrīcakra: each of its nine concentric parts, from the square to the point, with its presiding goddess (cakreśvarī), class of yoginīs, attendant deities and mudrā, worshipped in turn (navāvaraṇa-pūjā).

The central point of the Śrīcakra, abode of Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī, the ocean of nectar (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 8); in the Kāmakalāvilāsa the great point in which Śiva's light is reflected in the mirror of self-awareness, and the pair of white and red points.
The 'great point' formed when the rays of Paraśiva are reflected in the mirror of vimarśa; it is the 'I' (Kāmakalāvilāsa 4-5).
The central downward triangle of the Śrīcakra, the eighth enclosure, seat of Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī and Bhagamālinī (in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad the unmanifest, mahat and ahaṃkāra).
The outer square of the Śrīcakra with three lines and four gates, the first enclosure (trailokyamohana).
The nine 'wombs' (triangles) of the Śrīcakra — four of Śiva (śrīkaṇṭha) and five of Śakti (śivayuvatī) (SL 11; Tripurā Upaniṣad 2).
The triangle as womb of the universe: the triangles of the Śrīcakra are yonis; the yoni-mudrā is the ninth mudrā; the Tripurā Upaniṣad calls the Goddess's Śakti the womb of all.

The presiding goddess of each enclosure of the Śrīcakra: Tripurā, Tripureśī, Tripurasundarī, Tripuravāsinī, Tripurāśrī, Tripuramālinī, Tripurāsiddhā, Tripurāmbā and, at the centre, Mahātripurasundarī.

In Śrīvidyā the classes of attendant goddesses of the nine enclosures — Prakaṭa, Gupta, Guptatara, Sampradāya, Kulottīrṇa, Nigarbha, Rahasya, Atirahasya and Parāparātirahasya yoginīs; the Tripurā Upaniṣad (2) names nine yoginīs.
'The eternal ones': the fifteen goddesses of the lunar days (Kāmeśvarī to Citrā) around Tripurasundarī, the sixteenth (Mahānityā); they are the unfolding of time (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).

The eight goddesses of speech (Vaśinī, Kāmeśvarī, Modinī, Vimalā, Aruṇā, Jayinī, Sarveśvarī, Kaulinī) of the eight-cornered enclosure, composers of the Lalitā Sahasranāma; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad cold, heat, pleasure, pain, desire and the three qualities.
The fifteen-syllable Śrīvidyā mantra in three sections (kūṭa); called the 'full Gāyatrī' and given fifteen meanings in the Varivasyārahasya. (Syllables not recorded.)
The sixteen-syllable form of the Śrīvidyā ('the sixteen-syllable vidyā', LSN 118) and the Goddess named by it; the Bahvṛca Upaniṣad names her Ṣoḍaśī.
A 'peak' or section of the Śrīvidyā mantra; the three kūṭas (vāgbhava, kāmarāja/madhya, śakti) form the Goddess's subtle body from face to feet (LSN 35-36).
The first section of the mantra, 'born of speech'; the Goddess's face (LSN 35).
The middle section of the mantra; the Goddess's body from neck to waist (LSN 35).

literal: section of the king of desire

definitions.definition: The last section of the mantra; the Goddess's body below the waist (LSN 35).
The root mantra of the Goddess (the Śrīvidyā); she is 'of the nature of the root mantra' (LSN 36).

'Heart-letter': the name for the seed-syllable that closes each of the three sections of the vidyā (SL 32); the Varivasyārahasya analyses the subtle phases of its pronunciation. (Syllable not recorded.)
The form of the Śrīvidyā beginning with 'ka', called after Manmatha (Kāmarāja); the doctrine of the Tantrarāja ('Kādimata') and the form encoded in SL 32.
The form of the Śrīvidyā beginning with 'ha', called after Lopāmudrā; the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad says it teaches according to both Kādi and Hādi doctrines.
Bālā Tripurasundarī, the Goddess as a young girl, whose three-syllable vidyā is imparted first at initiation (PKS 1.39).
Śyāmā or Rājamātaṅgī, Lalitā's minister (Mantriṇī) who rides the Geyacakra chariot and slays Viṣaṅga (LSN 26-29); her worship is the sixth section of the Kalpasūtra.
Lalitā's general (Daṇḍanāthā, Daṇḍinī) on the Kiricakra chariot who slays Viśukra (LSN 26-30); her worship is the seventh section of the Kalpasūtra; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad she is 'the father'.
A goddess of the Śrīkula; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad 'the mother', deity of the offering; named in LSN 93.
The demon born from the ashes of Kāma burnt by Śiva, slain by Lalitā with her powers (LSN 25-33; Lalitopākhyāna).
The jewel island in the ocean of nectar, the Goddess's highest abode (SL 8; Devī Bhāgavata 12.10-12).
Lalitā's city on the central peak of Meru (LSN 22), with its enclosures described in the Lalitopākhyāna and the Āryādviśatī.
The palace of wish-gems at the centre of Śrīnagara, whose four doors are the four transmissions (PKS 3.10; LSN 22; SL 8).

The 'digit of desire': the white and red points, Śiva and Śakti, and the point of their union (the 'I'); kāma because it is lovely, kalā the two points of fire and moon; knowing this vidyā one becomes Mahātripurasundarī (KKV 6-8); the Goddess 'whose form is the kāmakalā' (LSN 73).
The 'I': the fusion of the first letter 'a' and the last 'ha', the union of Śiva and Śakti that holds the universe (KKV 5).
Light: Śiva's nature, 'whose body is pure light' (KKV 1); the Goddess is its fusion with self-awareness (Dīpikā on YH 1.6); Bhāskararāya's 'great light, seeing which nothing else is seen' (VR 3).
Self-awareness, the Goddess as the mirror in which Śiva knows himself (KKV 2); 'whose form is vimarśa' (LSN 112).
'Equal flavour', fusion: Tripurā is the sāmarasya of prakāśa and vimarśa (Dīpikā on YH 1.6); in the Varivasyārahasya one of the fifteen meanings of the mantra.
Consciousness-power: the Goddess as the power of the sentient, who is also the power of the insentient (LSN 90).
The power of will; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad it is Mahātripurasundarī herself, with the power of knowledge as her house and the power of action as her seat.
The power of knowledge; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad it is kuṇḍalinī, the Goddess's house.

notes: The Bhāvanā passage reads 'kuṇḍalinī jñānaśaktir gṛham'; the assignment of powers is as in the eBhāratī text.

definitions.definition: The power of action; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad it is the Goddess's seat (pīṭha).

The Goddess as the great power of māyā, who makes the universe whirl yet is the queen of the supreme Brahman (SL 98), who drags even the wise into delusion and when pleased grants liberation (Devī Māhātmya 1).
The Goddess's own power by which she becomes and veils the world; she is 'of the form of both knowledge and ignorance' (LSN 87) and 'the substratum of the illusory world' (LSN 142).
The five cosmic acts — creation, preservation, withdrawal, concealment and grace — performed by the Goddess through Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara and Sadāśiva (LSN 63-64; SL 24).
Concealment, the fourth cosmic act, done as Īśvarī (LSN 64).
Grace, the fifth cosmic act, bestowed as Sadāśiva (LSN 64).
The seat of five 'corpses' — Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and Īśvara as the legs and Sadāśiva as the plank of the Goddess's couch, lifeless without her (LSN 61; PKS 3.10; SL 94).
Witness: the Goddess is 'witness of the universe, without a witness' (LSN 84).
The fourth state beyond waking, dream and sleep; the Goddess is 'turyā' (LSN 63); in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad the fourth state is the prostration of inner worship.
The state beyond the fourth, reached by firmness in the fourth; the Goddess is 'devoid of all states' (Bhāskararāya on LSN 63).
Śiva clothed in body and coverings (PKS 1.5).
The 'jackets' covering Śiva and making him a jīva; without them he is Paraśiva (PKS 1.5).

Bond; the eight bonds beginning with disgust whose destruction is liberation while living (Dīpikā on YH 1.86); burned away by the guru at initiation (PKS 1.36); in the Goddess's hand the noose is attachment (LSN 2).
The bound soul; the Goddess's devotee is freed from 'the entanglement of the paśu's bonds' (SL 99).
Awareness of oneself, declared the goal of human life (PKS 1.6).

equivalents.note: knowledge of the self as the goal

definitions.definition: Being the self of all: liberation is its accomplishment (Kaula Upaniṣad).

Liberation while living, promised by knowledge of the cakra-code (YH 1.86) and of worship (YH 3.1), by three muhūrtas of the Bhāvanā contemplation, and to the steadfast practitioner who may die anywhere (PKS 10.82); the Dīpikā defines it as release from the eight bonds.
Union with the Goddess, granted to one who merely says 'Bhavāni tvam' (SL 22); the highest of the five liberations in Lakṣmīdhara.
The state of oneness granted by the Goddess ('giver of the state of kaivalya', LSN 125, 171).

notes: The Śākta sense (liberation as oneness with the Goddess) is only analogous to Pātañjala kaivalya (isolation of puruṣa); the two definitions should not be merged as one sense.

definitions.definition: The power of command that comes from firm contemplation (PKS 1.13).

The Goddess herself as the coiled power: dwelling in the mūlādhāra she pierces the three knots, mounts the thousand-petalled lotus, showers nectar, and returns to sleep in three and a half coils (LSN 38-40; SL 9-10).

equivalents.note: kuṇḍalinī is the Goddess in the body

definitions.definition: The three knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra that the Goddess pierces in her ascent (LSN 38-39).
The 'pit of kula' at the base of the spine where the Goddess sleeps coiled (SL 10); she 'dwells in the kula-pit' (LSN 93).
The thousand-petalled lotus of the crown where the Goddess unites with her consort (SL 9; LSN 39); for the Samayins the Śrīcakra is the moon-disc there (Lakṣmīdhara).
The root centre: the Goddess's sole dwelling (LSN 38); where the Samayin worships Samayā with Navātman (SL 41).

The navel centre, where the Goddess rises (LSN 38); the Saundaryalaharī assigns water to it (SL 9) and there worships the dark rain-cloud with its lightning (SL 40); the Samayins see the Goddess manifest there (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 7; Bhāskararāya on LSN 37).
Seat: the four seats Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara and Oḍḍiyāna, located in the subtle body (YH 1.41-42; LSN 82); the Goddess is 'of the form of the fifty seats', the letters (LSN 156).
One of the four great seats (pīṭha), which in the Yoginīhṛdaya are transformations of the four fused powers and are located in the subtle body.

notes: Shared with the Kaula pīṭha lists (U24).

definitions.definition: One of the four great seats (pīṭha), which in the Yoginīhṛdaya are transformations of the four fused powers and are located in the subtle body.

notes: Shared with the Kaula pīṭha lists (U24).

definitions.definition: One of the four great seats (pīṭha), which in the Yoginīhṛdaya are transformations of the four fused powers and are located in the subtle body.

notes: Shared with the Kaula pīṭha lists (U24).

definitions.definition: One of the four great seats (pīṭha), which in the Yoginīhṛdaya are transformations of the four fused powers and are located in the subtle body.

notes: Shared with the Kaula pīṭha lists (U24).

definitions.definition: The fifty letters as the 'little mothers', matrix of mantras; the Goddess is of the form of the fifty seats (LSN 156); mātṛkā is placed on the disciple's body at initiation (PKS 1.39).
The inner way: worship of the Śrīcakra in the space of the heart; also Śiva as 'Samaya', who has fivefold equality with the Goddess, 'Samayā' (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 8, 41).

Bhāskararāya: imagining the cakra in the dahara-space and worshipping there is called Samaya; the five tantras of Vasiṣṭha and the others are called Samaya; or Samaya is Śiva who shares fivefold equality with the Goddess (on LSN 37).
The Vedic, inner conduct of Śrīvidyā taught by the five Śubhāgamas and followed by Lakṣmīdhara; rejects outer and Kaula worship.
The Goddess is 'intent on Samaya conduct' (LSN 37); Bhāskararāya notes that the Rudrayāmala teaches samayācāra in ten chapters.
A follower of the Samaya way; for Samayins the worship is of Samayā and Samaya in the thousand-petalled lotus (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 41).
Kula is Śakti and akula Śiva; their relation is kaula; worship of the cakra drawn in outer space is conventionally called Kaula (Bhāskararāya on LSN 37).
Outer worship on a physical support, and the Kaula doctrines of the pūrva and uttara schools, which the Samaya way rejects (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 8, 23, 34-35).
The Kaula Upaniṣad's teaching: knowledge is the sole cause of liberation, which is being the self of all; inwardly Śākta, outwardly Śaiva, among people Vaiṣṇava.
Śakti; also the body, family, country and the lower thousand-petalled lotus (Bhāskararāya on LSN 36-37); the Goddess delights in kula-nectar and guards the kula conventions.
Śiva (in contrast with kula, Śakti); the Goddess is 'akulā', beyond kula (LSN 37).
The Goddess as Kaula, 'possessing kaula' — the fusion of Śiva and Śakti (Bhāskararāya); also the eighth goddess of speech.
The 'prior' Kaula view presented in Lakṣmīdhara's commentary on SL 34, on the Goddess as Śiva's body and the shared relation of principal and subsidiary.
The 'later' Kaula view, in which there is no Śiva-principle apart from the Śakti-principle and she alone is worshipped (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 23, 35).
The right-hand conduct; the Goddess 'abides on the right and left paths' and is 'worshipped by the dakṣiṇa and non-dakṣiṇa' (LSN 169-170).
The left-hand conduct, contrasted with the right; Lakṣmīdhara assigns it to those not eligible for the Vedic way.
Inner worship, in which knower, knowing and known are offerer, fire and oblation (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad; PKS 1.26); the Yoginīhṛdaya's inner worship is held sufficient for those firm in it (Setubandha).
Outer worship, e.g. of the Śrīcakra on a physical support; the Yoginīhṛdaya's 'aparā' worship, performed even by Śiva (YH 3.3).
Contemplative identification: the body as Śrīcakra and worship as non-difference (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad); its firmness brings the power of command (PKS 1.13); the Goddess is 'reached by bhāvanā' (LSN 41).
The small space of the heart where the Samayin imagines and worships the Śrīcakra (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 8; Bhāskararāya on LSN 37).
The 'secret sacrifice': the Goddess is worshipped by its sequence and pleased by secret libations (LSN 83). (Interpretations differ; summary only.)

The five 'M's — wine, meat, fish, parched grain or gesture, and sexual union — said to manifest the bliss that is Brahman's form; used in secret, and exposure leads to hell (PKS 1.12); daily worship continues without them when they are unavailable (PKS 1.24). Summary only.
A substitute used in place of a prescribed substance, notably for the five 'M's in the right-hand mode.
Initiation, threefold: śāktī by the entry of power, śāmbhavī by the placing of the foot, māntrī by mantra (PKS 1.32); Bālā is given first, with a name ending in '-ānandanātha' (PKS 1.39-41).

The guru's 'sandals' — the mantra of the guru's feet given before the Bālā (PKS 1.41); the feet are contemplated in the crown each morning (PKS 2.2); immersion in the Goddess's sandals is complete meditation (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
The ending of the initiatory name given to a Śrīvidyā initiate (PKS 1.40), as in Bhāsurānandanātha (Bhāskararāya).
The 'full consecration' of later Śrīvidyā manuals, conferring the full authority of the tradition after the preliminary initiations.
A 'stream' of gurus; Śrīvidyā worship honours three: the divine (divyaugha), the perfected (siddhaugha) and the human (mānavaugha) teachers, forming the circle of gurus.
The circle of gurus; the Goddess 'is of the form of the gurumaṇḍala' (LSN 138).
The tradition handed down; all success comes through tradition and faith (PKS 1.9); the Goddess is 'sovereign of the tradition' (LSN 138).
Faith or trust; validity 'consists above all in faith' (PKS 1.10).
A 'code' or 'tryst': the threefold saṅketa of cakra, mantra and worship (YH 1.6), explained as the meeting-place of Śiva and Śakti (Dīpikā).
The six levels of meaning of the mantra: bhāvārtha, sampradāyārtha, nigarbhārtha, kaulikārtha, sarvarahasyārtha, mahātattvārtha (YH 2.15-16).
A 'transmission' of teaching; Paramaśiva taught five āmnāyas through his five faces (PKS 1.2); the four doors of the Goddess's palace are the four āmnāyas (PKS 3.10).
The 'family of Śrī': the Śākta division centred on Tripurasundarī (Śrīvidyā), contrasted with the Kālīkula.
The five 'auspicious āgamas' (saṃhitās of Vasiṣṭha, Sanaka, Śuka, Sanandana and Sanatkumāra) that teach the Vedic Samaya way (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 31).
A service offered to the deity; the Goddess is 'rich in sixty-four services' (LSN 57); the Kalpasūtra lists them (PKS 4.5); the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad interiorizes them.
Libation that satisfies the deity; the Goddess is 'gratified by libation into the bindu' (LSN 178) and 'by secret libations' (LSN 83).
Seal: the ten mudrās of the Śrīcakra worship (sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī to trikhaṇḍā), one for each enclosure plus the tenth; the Goddess is 'worshipped with the ten mudrās' (LSN 179).
The tenth, three-part mudrā of Śrīvidyā worship; the Goddess is 'lady of the trikhaṇḍā' (LSN 180).
Placing mantras and deities on the body; Śrīvidyā uses many sets (karaśuddhi, the vāgdevatā-nyāsa, the sixfold ṣoḍhā-nyāsa and others), taught in the Vāmakeśvara and the Kalpasūtra.
The great sixfold placement of Śrīvidyā in which the worshipper becomes the deity's body; the Setubandha lists its components.
A married woman honoured as the Goddess; she is 'pleased by the worship of suvāsinīs' (LSN 178).
A young girl worshipped as the Goddess, especially in Navarātri (Devī Bhāgavata 3.26).
The nine nights of the Goddess's worship in autumn and spring (Devī Bhāgavata 3.26), each night associated with one of the nine Durgās (Devī Kavaca).
'The seven hundred': the Devī Māhātmya as recited in worship, with its limbs (kavaca, argalā, kīlaka, the three rahasyas).
The nine-syllable mantra of Caṇḍikā used with the Saptaśatī. (Syllables not recorded.)
'Hard to approach': the Goddess as the warrior who destroys demons and protects devotees; her nine forms are worshipped in Navarātri.
The fierce Goddess of the Devī Māhātmya.
'She whose eyes are desire' (LSN 23); the Goddess of Kāñcī, praised in the Mūka Pañcaśatī; by tradition Śaṅkara installed a Śrīcakra before her.
The 'great sacrifice': the Goddess is 'worshipped by the sequence of the great sacrifice' (LSN 56).
Recitation of the Goddess's names; she 'delights in the recitation of her names' (LSN 141), and the Rudrayāmala places it at the summit of a long ladder of births (Saubhāgyabhāskara).
Worship offering vermilion with each name of the Sahasranāma or Triśatī.
The last and timeless phase in the pronunciation of the mantra's final sound, beyond samanā (Varivasyārahasya).
The phase before unmanā in the subtle pronunciation of the mantra, lasting one unit (Varivasyārahasya).
Resonance: one of the subtle phases of the mantra's final sound, between rodhinī and nādānta (Varivasyārahasya).
The Vedic Gāyatrī read as Śrīvidyā (Tripurātāpinī Upaniṣad); the Pañcadaśī is called the 'full Gāyatrī' and its first meaning is the Gāyatrī meaning (VR 57); the Goddess is the Gāyatrī (LSN 90).
The 'hero', the qualified practitioner; the Goddess is 'mother of heroes' (LSN 156) and the knower of the mantra becomes 'lord of the circle of heroes' (YH 2.85).
